title: Kamini Ramani's 'Lotus Leadership' Asks: Where Are the Indian American Women?
excerpt: Silicon Valley executive Kamini Ramani's new book argues that Indian American women succeeded by drawing on their heritage — not by imitating men or 'leaning in.'
body:
• Kamini Ramani's Lotus Leadership: A Modern Playbook of Ancient Wisdom was published September 22, 2026, by HarperCollins, drawing on a year of interviews with more than 30 Indian-heritage women leaders in American business.
  • Its thesis: these women succeeded not by copying men's playbooks and not by Sheryl Sandberg-style "leaning in," but by unconsciously drawing on the stories of the Hindu goddesses they grew up with.
  • The book distills the pattern into a "Five Petals" framework — Fusion, Curiosity, Harmony, Abundance and Power — billed as a "yoga for business" anyone can practice.
  • How to engage: Ramani is discussing the book at Kepler's Literary Foundation with Judy Estrin and Srinija Srinivasan, followed by a book signing — check keplers.org for dates; the book is in bookshops now.

For decades, conversations about Indian American achievement have centered on the same men: the CEOs, the founders, the venture stars. Kamini Ramani — a 40-year veteran of Silicon Valley marketing who advised Steve Jobs and served as chief marketing officer of the Mayfield Fund — noticed something else. She had spent her career watching women of Indian heritage rise to the top of American business, and nobody was telling their story. So she spent a year interviewing more than 30 of them, and wrote the book herself.

The result, Lotus Leadership: A Modern Playbook of Ancient Wisdom, arrived in bookshops September 22, 2026. It draws on Ramani's own arc — Bombay to JFK in 1983, Yale and Stanford, counsel to Steve Jobs at NeXT, and CMO of Mayfield Fund — but it is mostly the story of the women she found.

The argument: not lean in, but lead differently

The book's central claim, per its Publishers Weekly starred review: the women Ramani studied did not succeed by following the playbook of (white or Indian) men, nor by Sheryl Sandberg's 2013 "lean in" model. Instead, they drew, often unconsciously, on the learned wisdom of their heritage: specifically, the stories of the main Hindu goddesses they were raised with. At the core, she argues, is an embrace of duality that encourages harmony over dissonance, an emphasis on the collective over the individual, and the ability to own power with calm and resilience.

Ramani organizes these traits into what she calls the Five Petals of Lotus Leadership: Fusion (embracing so-called feminine and masculine sides in harmony, rooted in the Shiva-Shakti philosophy), Curiosity (letting curiosity, not titles or paychecks, guide you), Harmony (building life partnerships that take a long view of "having it all"), Abundance (measuring wealth to include family, team, philanthropy and community), and Power (combining the traits in a way unique to your own journey). She likens the whole practice to a "yoga for business" that anyone, of any background, can follow.

"I've met so many amazing women leaders. I wanted to understand both their professional journeys and the ways they approached leadership."

— Kamini Ramani, author of Lotus Leadership

The women at the book's heart

The empirical core of the book is a year of deep listening with 30 leaders Ramani found remarkable — not a randomized study, but qualitative interviews drawn from her own professional network. Among the profiles documented in the Publishers Weekly review: Aparna Bawa, the chief operating officer of Zoom, whom Ramani uses to illustrate grit developed growing up in a society that prioritizes boys over girls — the ability to perform amid chaos that helped her helm Zoom as its user base skyrocketed during the COVID-19 pandemic. And Geetha Murali, CEO of the children's literacy nonprofit Room to Read, portrayed as embodying the Shiva-Shakti fusion: blending strategy and analysis with empathy and emotion.

Ramani's own credentials run through the work. A founding member of Neythri — the global network for South Asian professional women — she has spent four decades inside Silicon Valley's formal power structure and its informal South Asian women's support ecosystem. She is a 35-year San Francisco resident, married to Omar Khan, with two adult daughters.

What this means for the diaspora

For young Indian American women entering corporate life, Lotus Leadership offers a permission structure that is neither assimilation nor rebellion: succeed as you are, because what you carry is the asset. For managers and mentors, it is a case study in how culturally formed leadership styles can outperform the default playbook.

Diaspora readers can catch her in conversation at Kepler's Literary Foundation, where she appears with Judy Estrin and Srinija Srinivasan ahead of a book signing, and through her official site for speaking and media inquiries. The audiobook, read by Ramani herself, is also available.

What to watch

The open question is whether the leadership market — dominated since 2013 by the "lean in" conversation — has room for a sustained counter-argument. Ramani asserts the framework is universal; whether the Shiva-Shakti duality travels beyond women raised in that tradition will decide whether Lotus Leadership becomes a book the diaspora cites, or one it canonizes.
